analysis.one_liner: Creates a government health plan covering every U.S. resident with no premiums, deductibles, or copays, and outlaws duplicate private insurance.
analysis.headline: All 116 cosponsors plus the sponsor are House Democrats, but after being referred to seven committees in April 2025, no committee has acted and no vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would replace private health insurance and most existing federal health programs with a single government-run plan covering everyone in the United States. It would cover hospital care, prescription drugs, mental health and substance use treatment, dental, vision, reproductive care, gender-affirming care, and long-term care, and would ban deductibles, copays, coinsurance, balance billing, and prior authorization. Private insurers and employers could only sell coverage for extras not already covered. The program would phase in over two years, with children and people 55 and older covered first, and others able to buy in during the transition.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident gains guaranteed, comprehensive health coverage with no out-of-pocket charges: no premiums, no deductibles, no copays, no surprise bills, and no insurance-company approval needed before getting care. Families currently skipped or priced out of coverage, people with preexisting conditions who face high premiums, older adults before age 65, and people needing dental, vision, or long-term care that most plans skip today would benefit most. Workers would no longer be tied to a job for insurance, and the bill provides transition help for insurance-industry workers whose jobs disappear [S2, S3].

how_it_helps.text: Every U.S. resident is entitled to benefits, with automatic enrollment at birth or upon establishing residency, so no one can be uninsured for lacking money or job-based coverage.

The bill bans cost-sharing of any kind — deductibles, coinsurance, copayments — plus balance billing and prior authorization or step-therapy limits, ending the out-of-pocket costs and coverage denials that drive medical debt today.

The benefits package is far broader than typical job-based insurance: hospital care, prescription drugs, mental health and substance use treatment, dental, audiology, and vision services, long-term care at home or in a facility, comprehensive reproductive care including abortion, gender-affirming care, and hospice.
Patients could see any qualified provider, with no networks to navigate, and the bill requires negotiated prescription drug prices.
Coverage phases in over two years, starting with people 55 and older and children under 19 one year after enactment, with an option for others to buy in during the transition.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers as a whole: the single public plan would be funded through the federal Universal Medicare Trust Fund, meaning the premiums, deductibles, and copays families and employers pay today would be replaced by federal taxes. The provided bill text establishes the trust fund but does not spell out the specific taxes that would raise the money. Hospitals would have their payments set by negotiated annual global budgets instead of billed charges, and hospitals and providers would face new conflict-of-interest and compensation rules. Health insurers lose the market for core coverage, though they may still sell supplemental policies.

drawbacks.text: The bill outlaws private insurance that duplicates the public plan and stops employers from offering job-based coverage, so everyone's current coverage would end and be replaced — a genuine disruption for people satisfied with what they have today.

Total federal health spending and the taxes to fund it would be very large; the bill text provided establishes the Universal Medicare Trust Fund but does not detail the revenue sources that would pay for it, leaving the financing question open.

Hospitals would be paid through negotiated global budgets capped by the national health budget, which constrains their revenue and could limit expansion or cause cash-flow strain during the two-year transition.

The transition would be a heavy administrative lift: exchanges and federal health programs terminate, and workers in insurance administration face job loss (the bill sets aside 1% of the budget for up to five years for wage replacement and retraining for them).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit for ordinary people is large and direct: universal coverage with zero out-of-pocket costs and a wider benefits package than most Americans have now. The cost is equally real: it is one of the biggest single changes Congress could make, shifting the entire financing of American health care from premiums and employer benefits to federal taxes, and the two-year transition — ending every existing plan and standing up a new payment system — carries serious execution risk. Whether the trade is favorable depends heavily on how the taxes that fund it are designed, which this bill text leaves open.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2025 and sent to seven House committees, and none has taken it up since — so it sits with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote scheduled while the Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on April 29, 2025 by Rep. Pramila Jayapal.

It was referred to seven House committees at once — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and Workforce, Rules, Oversight and Government Reform, Armed Services, and Judiciary — with no action taken by any of them since.
All 116 cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on.
As of the latest action history, the bill has had no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the status quo is preserved: private health insurers, employers' benefit plans, and drug makers keep the current system, and the 26 million-plus uninsured remain so. The 117 House Democrats backing the bill have so far gained nothing for their constituents.

sides.party_line_note: All 117 sponsors and cosponsors are House Democrats and no Republican has cosponsored, and with Republicans holding the House majority, no committee or floor action has occurred.

industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful to sell insurance that duplicates the public plan, and the Affordable Care Act exchanges are sunset — insurers would be left with only supplemental coverage. Their revenue depends on the current system of premiums, deductibles, and coverage denials that the bill eliminates for patients.
The bill requires HHS to negotiate prescription drug prices, replacing the current system where manufacturers largely set U.S. prices. Patients would pay nothing out of pocket for covered drugs.
Employers would be barred from providing coverage that duplicates the public plan, ending the job-based insurance system most workers rely on — but they also stop paying a large share of premiums.

Hospitals lose billed charges and private-insurer reimbursement but gain guaranteed payment for every patient through negotiated global budgets, and uncompensated care ends. Conflict-of-interest and compensation caps constrain hospital executives.

industries.industry: Health insurance administrative and billing sector
industries.note: A single-payer system needs a fraction of the claims-processing workforce; the bill funds up to five years of wage replacement, retraining, and preferential hiring for displaced workers from 1% of the health budget.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding the House majority, no Republican cosponsors, and no committee action seven months after referral to seven committees, the bill is very unlikely to get a hearing or vote in this Congress and would expire in January 2027 unless reintroduced. Versions of it have been introduced in every recent Congress with the same result: strong Democratic cosponsorship, no Republican support, and death in committee.
